decks.domain: Missouri special driving conditions: night driving and headlights, winter driving, wet pavement and hydroplaning, anti-lock brakes, skids, fog and vehicle emergencies

cards.front: Why is driving at night harder than driving in daylight?
cards.back: Night driving is harder because headlights show less of the road ahead and to the sides than daylight does, and oncoming glare makes the road harder to see.

cards.front: During which hours of the day must your headlights be on?
cards.back: Headlights must be on from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise.
cards.memory_hook: half hour after sunset, before sunrise

cards.front: Besides darkness, what weather condition makes Missouri require headlights?
cards.back: Missouri requires headlights any time the weather calls for using your windshield wipers.

cards.front: What are the two separate triggers that require headlights in Missouri?
cards.back: Headlights are required by the clock from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise, and also by the weather whenever the wipers are needed.

cards.front: How should you care for your windows and headlights for night driving?
cards.back: Keep windows and headlights clean, make sure the lights work, and have their aim checked from time to time.

cards.front: When should you use your high beams?
cards.back: Use high beams whenever no vehicles are coming toward you.

cards.front: How far ahead do headlights let you see, and how should that limit your speed?
cards.back: Headlights let you see only about three hundred fifty feet ahead, so do not overdrive them; keep a speed at which you can stop or turn within that range.

cards.front: How close to an oncoming vehicle, and to a vehicle you follow, must you dim to low beams?
cards.back: Dim to low beams within five hundred feet, about one block, of an oncoming vehicle, and within three hundred feet when following another vehicle.

cards.front: Which three night distances are easy to mix up, and what is each one?
cards.back: Three night distances are easy to mix up: headlights reach about three hundred fifty feet, you dim for oncoming traffic at five hundred feet, and you dim when following within three hundred feet.

cards.front: At night, what line should you follow and what should you watch for beside the road?
cards.back: At night, follow the edgeline, or the center line if there is no edgeline, and watch for signs and for people and vehicles stopped beside the road.

cards.front: What should you do for curves at night if you are already at the posted maximum?
cards.back: Slow down for curves at night if you are already driving at the posted maximum.

cards.front: What does the guide say about alertness and tiredness for night driving?
cards.back: Stay awake and alert at night and do not drive if you feel tired.

cards.front: Which two pieces of equipment should you check before winter driving?
cards.back: Before winter driving, make sure the windshield wipers and defroster both work.

cards.front: What must you clear in winter before setting off, and when may you leave?
cards.back: In winter clear all snow and ice from the windows, headlights and taillights, and never set off, however short the trip, until the windows are clear.

cards.front: What do snow-rated tires or chains change about driving on snow or ice?
cards.back: Snow-rated tires or chains help, but no vehicle can be driven safely on snow or ice at normal speeds, so slow down and do not use cruise control.

cards.front: What should you keep ready if your vehicle lacks snow-rated tires?
cards.back: If your vehicle lacks snow-rated tires, keep chains ready to put on in bad weather.

cards.front: How should you accelerate when starting out on snow or ice?
cards.back: When starting out on snow or ice, accelerate slowly and smoothly.

cards.front: What should you do if your tires spin when you start on snow?
cards.back: If your tires spin when starting on snow, rock gently back and forth to clear a path, then spread salt, sand or cat litter around the wheels if needed.

cards.front: Why must nobody stand in line with spinning wheels?
cards.back: Never let anyone stand in line with spinning wheels, because they can throw gravel or ice and hurt someone.

cards.front: Once moving on snow or ice, how do you judge how slippery the road is?
cards.back: Once moving on snow or ice, brake gently to test how slippery the road is and set your speed to match.

decks.module: Stopping and ice on winter roads
decks.domain: Missouri special driving conditions: night driving and headlights, winter driving, wet pavement and hydroplaning, anti-lock brakes, skids, fog and vehicle emergencies

cards.front: On snow or ice, how much following time should you leave to the vehicle ahead?
cards.back: On snow or ice, stopping takes longer, so leave about eight to ten seconds between you and the vehicle ahead.

cards.front: How does the safe gap to the vehicle ahead change on snow or ice, and why?
cards.back: On snow or ice the safe gap to the vehicle ahead grows to about eight to ten seconds, because stopping takes longer.

cards.front: How should you brake on slippery roads, and what does the guide say about very slick surfaces?
cards.back: Brake gently and smoothly on slippery roads; slamming the brakes can cause a skid, and on very slick surfaces you pump the brakes unless your manual gives anti-lock instructions.

cards.front: Which parts of the road freeze first, and where else can ice hide?
cards.back: Bridges and overpasses freeze before the rest of the road, and patches of ice may remain even on cleared roads.

cards.front: What does the guide say about four-wheel drive on ice?
cards.back: Do not use four-wheel drive on ice, where such vehicles can easily roll over; if you hit ice in four-wheel drive, lift your foot off the accelerator.

decks.domain: Missouri special driving conditions: night driving and headlights, winter driving, wet pavement and hydroplaning, anti-lock brakes, skids, fog and vehicle emergencies

cards.front: What happens to the road when rain starts, and how should you respond?
cards.back: When rain starts, water mixes with road dust and oil into a slick film, wet leaves turn slippery, and stopping takes longer, so slow down and add following distance.

cards.front: What does wet pavement do to driving through curves?
cards.back: Wet pavement also makes it harder to stay on the road through curves.

cards.front: Why should you not use cruise control on wet pavement?
cards.back: Do not use cruise control on wet pavement, because it keeps powering the wheels after traction is lost and can make you lose control.

cards.front: What is hydroplaning, and at what speeds can it happen?
cards.back: Hydroplaning is when tires ride on water instead of the road; it can happen at any speed over thirty-five miles per hour, and in a heavy storm tires can lose all contact at fifty-five miles per hour

cards.front: Which speed marks the start of hydroplaning, and which marks full loss of contact in a severe storm?
cards.back: Hydroplaning can begin above thirty-five miles per hour, while full loss of road contact in a severe storm can come at fifty-five miles per hour

cards.front: What should you do if you think you are hydroplaning?
cards.back: If you think you are hydroplaning, ease off the accelerator and slow down without braking, which could cause a skid.

cards.front: How do you prevent hydroplaning?
cards.back: Prevent hydroplaning with good, deep-tread tires at proper pressure, slower speeds in rain, and no cruise control.

decks.domain: Missouri special driving conditions: night driving and headlights, winter driving, wet pavement and hydroplaning, anti-lock brakes, skids, fog and vehicle emergencies

cards.front: What do four-wheel anti-lock brakes do, and what might you feel under hard braking?
cards.back: Four-wheel anti-lock brakes keep the wheels from locking in emergency braking, and you may feel the pedal pulse under hard braking.

cards.front: How do you use anti-lock brakes in a hard stop?
cards.back: With anti-lock brakes, keep firm, steady pressure on the pedal while you steer; do not pump the brakes, and do not be alarmed by mechanical noise or slight pulsing.

cards.front: What does the winter page say about pumping on very slippery surfaces, and how does it treat anti-lock vehicles?
cards.back: On very slippery surfaces the winter page says to pump the brakes, but for a vehicle with anti-lock brakes it points you to the owner's manual for special situations.

cards.front: Does handling a skid differ between front-wheel and rear-wheel drive, and what are the first steps?
cards.back: A skid is handled the same way in front-wheel and rear-wheel drive vehicles: lift off the accelerator and do not hit the brakes.

cards.front: Which way do you steer in a skid, and what should you avoid?
cards.back: In a skid, gently steer in the direction the rear wheels are sliding, without braking hard or jerking the wheel, which only makes it worse.

cards.front: What four steps does the guide's skid diagram caption?
cards.back: The guide's skid diagram is captioned in four steps: before the skid, rear wheels sliding right, front wheels turned right, and the vehicle straight again.

decks.domain: Missouri special driving conditions: night driving and headlights, winter driving, wet pavement and hydroplaning, anti-lock brakes, skids, fog and vehicle emergencies

cards.front: How should you drive in fog, and which beams should you use?
cards.back: In fog, slow down, be ready to stop, and use low beams, because high beams make it harder to see.

cards.front: What should you do if fog gets so thick that you cannot see?
cards.back: If fog gets so thick that you cannot see, pull off the road, stop, and leave your lights and emergency flashers on.

cards.front: What is the most important rule in any emergency, and when may you turn off the ignition?
cards.back: The most important rule in any emergency is not to panic, and with power steering or a locking steering wheel, never turn off the ignition until fully stopped.

cards.front: How does staying calm help you in an emergency?
cards.back: Staying calm in an emergency helps you remember what to do.

cards.front: What should you do if the brake pedal sinks to the floor?
cards.back: If the brake pedal sinks to the floor, pump it fast and hard several times, then apply the parking brake gradually and shift to a low gear while looking for a place to stop.

cards.front: Which emergency calls for pumping the pedal fast and hard, and how does that differ from anti-lock braking?
cards.back: Brake failure is the one emergency here where you pump the pedal fast and hard, which is the opposite of the steady pressure used with working anti-lock brakes.

cards.front: What should you do with the vehicle after a brake failure?
cards.back: After a brake failure, get the vehicle off the road and call for help instead of driving to a garage.

cards.front: How might a tire blowout announce itself?
cards.back: A blowout may announce itself with a loud bang followed by a repeated thumping, and the steering wheel may jerk.

cards.front: How do you handle a tire blowout, and when may you brake?
cards.back: In a tire blowout, grip the wheel firmly, lift off the accelerator without braking, and let the car slow until it is nearly stopped and off the road before braking.

cards.front: After a blowout, what should you turn on, and when should you change the tire?
cards.back: After a blowout, turn on the emergency flashers and change the tire only if you can do it without putting yourself in danger.

cards.front: What should you do if your wheels drop off the paved edge?
cards.back: If your wheels drop off the paved edge, hold the wheel tightly, ease off the gas without braking hard, and steer back once you have slowed, have control and the lane is clear.

cards.front: Which way may the wheels pull when they run off the paved edge, and how should you brake?
cards.back: When wheels run off the paved edge, they may pull to the right, so hold the wheel firmly and use only gentle braking if any is needed.

cards.front: What should you do if the steering fails?
cards.back: If the steering fails, lift off the accelerator, let the vehicle slow on its own without braking until nearly stopped unless you must, and turn on the flashers.

cards.front: When do you brake after a blowout, and when after a steering failure?
cards.back: After a blowout you brake only when nearly stopped, and after a steering failure you also wait to brake until nearly stopped unless you must.

cards.front: What should you do if your headlights fail?
cards.back: If the headlights fail, try the dimmer or headlight switch, then switch on parking lights, flashers or turn signals and pull off the road with the flashers left on.

cards.front: What should you do if the hood flies up or the wipers fail?
cards.back: If the hood flies up or the wipers fail, roll down the window to see around the blockage, turn on the flashers and pull off the road.

decks.module: Stuck pedals, head-on, tracks and vans
decks.domain: Missouri special driving conditions: night driving and headlights, winter driving, wet pavement and hydroplaning, anti-lock brakes, skids, fog and vehicle emergencies

cards.front: What steps does the guide give for a stuck accelerator?
cards.back: For a stuck accelerator, shift to neutral, brake, keep watching the road, warn others with the horn and flashers, and steer safely off the road.

cards.front: With a stuck accelerator, when may you turn off the ignition, and why wait?
cards.back: With a stuck accelerator, turn off the ignition only after stopping and no longer needing to steer, since turning off the key locks the steering in many vehicles.

cards.front: What should you keep looking for while slowing with a stuck accelerator?
cards.back: With a stuck accelerator, keep looking for a way out of traffic while you slow down.

cards.front: How does the braking response to a stuck accelerator differ from a blowout?
cards.back: A stuck accelerator calls for shifting to neutral and braking right away, unlike a blowout, where you avoid the brakes at first.

cards.front: What should you do if a vehicle comes at you head-on in your lane?
cards.back: If a vehicle comes at you head-on in your lane, slow down, pull to the right and sound your horn, but do not swerve into the left lane.

cards.front: Why is swerving into the left lane dangerous when a vehicle comes at you head-on?
cards.back: Swerving into the left lane to avoid a head-on vehicle is dangerous because the other driver may move back into that same lane.

cards.front: If you stall on railroad tracks with a train coming, what do you do and which way do you run?
cards.back: If your vehicle stalls on railroad tracks with a train coming, unbuckle, get out and away from the tracks, running toward the direction the train is coming from to avoid flying debris.

cards.front: Why is running in the direction the train is heading dangerous after a stall?
cards.back: Running in the direction the train is heading after a stall puts you in the path of debris when the train strikes your vehicle.

cards.front: If you stall on the tracks with no train in sight, what steps should you take?
cards.back: If you stall on the tracks with no train in sight, roll down the windows to listen, try to restart, and if that fails, shift to neutral and push the vehicle off.

cards.front: What has the NTSB found about large passenger vans, and what does it recommend?
cards.back: The NTSB has found that twelve- and fifteen-passenger vans are inherently unstable when loaded as designed with more than ten passengers, and it recommends special training for their drivers.

cards.front: Where does the NTSB point drivers of large passenger vans for more on van safety?
cards.back: The NTSB points drivers of large passenger vans to its website for more on van safety.

recap_hooks.text: Headlights go on from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise, and also whenever the weather calls for wipers.
You see about three hundred fifty feet in your lights, so do not outrun them; dim at five hundred feet for oncoming cars and three hundred when following.
Use high beams when no one is coming, follow the edgeline, slow for night curves and stay off the road when tired.
Before winter, check wipers and defroster and clear snow and ice from windows, headlights and taillights before any trip.
Snow tires or chains help, but slow down, skip cruise control and start out slowly and smoothly.
Rock gently to free spinning tires, keep people out of line with them, and test the road with a gentle brake once moving.

recaps.module: Stopping and ice on winter roads

recap_hooks.text: On snow or ice, stopping takes longer, so leave about eight to ten seconds to the car ahead.
Brake gently, pump on very slick surfaces unless your manual says otherwise, expect bridges to freeze first, and leave four-wheel drive off the ice.
The first rain leaves a slick film, curves get harder and cruise control can keep powering wheels that have lost grip.
Hydroplaning can start above thirty-five miles per hour and become full loss of contact at fifty-five in a heavy storm.
If you hydroplane, ease off without braking; prevent it with deep tread, proper pressure, slower speeds and no cruise control.
Anti-lock brakes stop the wheels from locking: press firmly and steadily, steer, and ignore the noise and pulsing.
The winter page says pump on very slick surfaces, but anti-lock owners check the manual.
In any skid, lift off the gas, skip the brakes and steer gently where the rear wheels slide until the car is straight.
In fog, slow down with low beams; if you cannot see, pull off and leave lights and flashers on.
Do not panic, stay calm, and keep the ignition on until fully stopped.
A pedal that sinks gets pumped fast and hard, then the parking brake and a low gear; afterward, call for help.
A bang and thumping mean a blowout: grip the wheel, coast without braking, and brake only when nearly stopped and off the road.
Off the paved edge or with failed steering, ease off and slow before steering back or braking.
Failed headlights or a raised hood call for flashers and pulling off the road.

recaps.module: Stuck pedals, head-on, tracks and vans

recap_hooks.text: A stuck accelerator means neutral and brakes right away, unlike a blowout; the ignition goes off only after you stop.
For a head-on car in your lane, slow, pull right and honk rather than swerving left.
Stalled with a train coming, get out and run toward the direction it comes from; with no train in sight, try to restart or push off in neutral.
